_source.displaydescription:
Four aniconic stone statues representing various deities are established inside the Pīṭha. They are adorned with toraṇa, one of which is larger than the others.

The local community worships it as the Indrāyaṇī. There is another kīrtimukhatoraṇa behind this statue and a large tree growing behind the Pīṭha. A phalcā and a hiti is constructed nearby the temple.

Indrāyaṇī’s statue, brought from the deity’s god-house (dyaḥchẽ), is exhibited here during auspicious occasions. Thrice every year, the deity’s chariot procession is organised and is taken around the city quarters of the core city.

The local community, especially from the western part of Bhaktapur, come here to worship on their birthdays and conduct kalaḥpūjā . Devotees throng to the temple on the eighth, ninth, and tenth day of Dasaĩ festival. Some of them also offer animal sacrifice during Dasaĩ.

_source.displaydescription:
Siddhimāna Rājabhaṇḍārī constructed the temple at the Pacalī Ghāṭa in the memory of his father Siddhinārāyaṇa Rājabhaṇḍārī in 1854 CE. Siddhimāna also constructed Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa (KAT2636) and Dhaneśvara Mandira (KAT2638). The temple was consecrated on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Māgha in 1855 CE (VS 1911). A stone śivaliṅga, which was brought from India, is consecrated as the main deity inside its sanctum.

Siddhimāna was one of the trusted elites of Jaṅga Bahādura Rāṇā and fiercely supported the Rāṇā regime. He was a subbā in 1846 CE, and in 1859 CE, he became a treasurer (khajāñcī). He was appointed as the governor for Banke, Bardiya, Kailali, and Kanchanpur districts, collectively known as the Nayā Muluka ‘New Kingdom’ in 1864 CE. Siddhimāna played a significant role in the economic upliftment of these districts (Adhikari 1984, 219). He also accompanied Jaṅga Bahādura to his official state visit to the Great Britain in 1850 CE (Rana 1974, 116).

He had also established a guṭhī and endowed land to sustain the daily worship in this temple. However, neither the endowed land nor the guṭhī exist in the present-day. Previously, a Brahmin priest was appointed as the priest to perform the daily rituals and he was paid a monthly salary of four thousand rupees. In the present-day, Viṣṇudevī Rājabhaṇḍārī, Siddhimāna Rājabhaṇḍārī’s fifth-generation daughter-in-law, performs the daily worship in the temple. She also operates a home for elderly in the temple premises.

The anniversary celebration of the temple takes place every year on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha. On the day of Śivarātri, a big light (mahādīpa) is lit in the temple premises and a special worship is performed on the birthday of Kṛṣṇa (Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī). A person called Rāmacandra Thāpā, who runs a paint shop in Ṭeku, Kathmandu, has been painting and repairing the temple from time to time.
